angle: We thought we knew our ICP. Our closed-won data said otherwise
post_first_line: Our ICP was wrong. Closed-won data said so.
linkedin_post:
Our ICP was wrong. Closed-won data said so.

The gap between who we assumed we sold to and who actually bought was bigger than I expected.

We thought our ICP was pretty standard: a set of top segments and the kinds of businesses we sell into.

Then we looked back at our closed-won customers. We pulled the conversation intelligence from those deals and read the transcripts, looking for particular moments.

One of them was a recent product launch.

If a company had just launched a product, they were looking at Unify at a higher clip.

That's not a segment on a slide. It's a moment in time. And it's something a static ICP list never captures.

What I took from it: your ICP isn't only who the company is. It's also what's happening to them right now.

The closed-won transcripts told us more than our assumptions did.

What signal showed up in your closed-won deals?

lesson.title: Your ICP is a moment, not just a segment
takeaways: Assumed ICPs often reflect habit, not closed-won evidence.
Conversation transcripts from won deals reveal moments that predict buying interest.
A trigger like a recent product launch can matter as much as firmographics.
lesson.exercise: Pull transcripts from your last 10 closed-won deals and list every recurring moment or event the buyer mentioned. Pick the most common one and test it as a targeting signal.

angle: How to launch an automated outbound play without sending anything embarrassing
post_first_line: Delay your launch by 10 to 20 minutes.
linkedin_post:
Delay your launch by 10 to 20 minutes.

That one setting is how I keep automated outbound from sending anything embarrassing.

Before a play goes live, I've already tested the agents and the snippets at a smaller scale. But small-scale tests don't catch everything.

So when we launch, I delay the sequence. You can do this natively in Unify. Then I read through the sample emails and check the accuracy. I'm looking for anything wacky.

Sometimes a sample reply comes back saying "we didn't launch this product" or "this is from months ago." When that happens, I tweak the agent and keep testing.

Edge cases will still slip through. We probably get one every few thousand emails.

Based on the results, it's well worth it.

The goal isn't zero mistakes. It's catching the systematic ones before they hit thousands of inboxes.

What's your pre-launch check for automated outreach?

Slide 2: Test your agents and snippets at small scale first
Slide 3: At launch, delay the sequence by 10 to 20 minutes
Slide 4: Read through the sample emails and check accuracy
Slide 5: Watch for outdated claims or products you never launched
Slide 6: Found something off? Tweak the agent and keep testing
Slide 7: Expect an edge case every few thousand emails
Slide 8: Catch the systematic errors before they scale

lesson.title: Launching an automated outbound play safely
takeaways: Small-scale testing of agents and snippets comes before any full launch.
Delaying the sequence 10 to 20 minutes gives you a window to review real sample emails.
Edge cases are inevitable, roughly one every few thousand, but worth the tradeoff given the results.
lesson.exercise: For your next automated play, add a 20-minute delay at launch, read 10 sample emails for accuracy, and note any fix the agent needs before the delay ends.

caption: Delay launch. Check everything.

angle: The boring first-party signal still booking 20+ meetings a month: someone sitting on your pricing page
post_first_line: 20+ meetings last month from one signal.
linkedin_post:
20+ meetings last month from one signal.

It's not a fancy one, and it's not a new one.

Someone sitting on our pricing page. That's still one of the most successful signals we have. Last month, website intent plus prospecting into those accounts drove over 20 meetings.

The rest of our first-party stack is just as unglamorous:

- MQLs that come in from gated content
- People viewing our product tour
- CRM data, like close lost opportunities sorted by loss reason

Everyone wants the clever third-party trigger. Meanwhile, the people already on your site, showing high intent, are the ones getting ignored.

I'd start with what buyers are already doing on your own properties before buying another data source.

angle: Our AI signal kept flagging pricing changes as 'major launches.' Here's the fix.
post_first_line: Pricing changes are not major launches.
linkedin_post:
Pricing changes are not major launches.

My AI signal didn't know that, and it took testing to catch it.

I built a signal to flag when a company ships a major launch. In early tests, it kept pulling in things we would never call a launch.

Pricing changes. Internal tools. Internal hiring news.

The model wasn't broken. My definition of "major launch" was vague, so it filled the gaps on its own.

The fix was giving it specific criteria and structure.

What counts: a major feature, a significant go-to-market shift, or a net new customer-facing product.

What to ignore: things like pricing-only announcements.

If your signal is noisy, the prompt is usually the problem. Define what counts and what doesn't, and the output gets a lot cleaner.

What's the noisiest signal in your stack right now?
carousel: Slide 1: My AI signal kept calling pricing changes major launches.
Slide 2: It also flagged internal tools and hiring news as launches.
Slide 3: The model wasn't broken. My definition was too vague.
Slide 4: Vague criteria means the AI fills the gaps itself.
Slide 5: So I defined what counts: major feature, GTM shift, new product.
Slide 6: Then I defined what to ignore: pricing-only announcements.
Slide 7: Specific criteria plus structure gave a much cleaner signal.
Slide 8: Noisy signal? Fix the definition before you blame the model.

lesson.title: Define 'major launch' before your AI does it for you
takeaways: Testing early surfaces false positives like pricing changes, internal tools, and hiring news.
Vague terms like 'major launch' get interpreted loosely unless you give criteria and structure.
Spell out both what counts (major feature, GTM shift, net new customer-facing product) and what to ignore (pricing-only announcements).
lesson.exercise: Pull 10 recent outputs from one of your AI signals and mark the false positives. Then rewrite the prompt with an explicit 'counts' list and an 'ignore' list based on those misses.

angle: The buying signals we watch when the real pain isn't public
post_first_line: Hiring heavily for BD? That's a pipeline problem.
linkedin_post:
Hiring heavily for BD? That's a pipeline problem.

Most of the best buying signals aren't announced anywhere. Nobody posts "our pipeline is broken."

So I look at what a company does instead of what it says. Hiring is the clearest one. If a team is hiring heavily for BD, they probably need more pipeline.

Then I open the job description. It gives a sense of their tech stack, which tells me about their current workflow and the potential pains I can go after.

Headcount growth is another one. So is divestment in certain areas.

What counts as a signal will look different depending on the type of business. But the pattern holds: lean on external signals and infer from there.

You're not waiting for a company to tell you the pain. You're reading it from the outside.

What's the best non-obvious signal you track?
carousel: Slide 1: The real pain is rarely public. Read the signals instead.
Slide 2: Hiring a ton for BD? They probably need more pipeline.
Slide 3: Open the job description. It's more than a role listing.
Slide 4: The JD hints at their tech stack and current workflow.
Slide 5: Workflow gaps point to potential pains you can go after.
Slide 6: Headcount growth and divestment in certain areas are signals too.
Slide 7: Signals look different for every type of business.
Slide 8: Use external signals, then infer the pain from there.

lesson.title: Inferring Buyer Pain From External Signals
takeaways: Heavy hiring for a BD team suggests a company probably needs more pipeline.
Job descriptions reveal tech stack, which hints at current workflow and potential pains.
Headcount growth and divestment in certain areas are signals worth tracking, and they vary by business type.
lesson.exercise: Pick five target accounts. For each, read one open job description and write down the tech stack mentioned, the workflow it implies, and one pain you could plausibly address.

angle: Spotting the signal is only half the job. The other half is the message
post_first_line: Half the signal workflow is the message.
linkedin_post:
Half the signal workflow is the message.

Most teams stop at detecting the trigger and miss where the leverage actually sits.

Quintin Smith made a point that gets overlooked: the power isn't only in turning signals into intent triggers that fire specific plays. It's also in the customization of the copy.

You get two things working together. Always-on monitoring for the trigger, and outreach that's personalized to it.

That means no seller has to look at an intent signal, then go build the copy by hand. Both pieces are automated.

A signal without a relevant message is just a notification. A message without a signal is just a guess.

Personalization that's hyper relevant at scale only happens when the trigger and the copy are connected.

Where does your signal workflow break down: detection or messaging?
carousel: Slide 1: Spotting the signal is only half the job.
Slide 2: The other half is the message that follows it.
Slide 3: Signals can trigger specific plays automatically.
Slide 4: Always-on monitoring catches the trigger without manual checking.
Slide 5: The copy gets customized to that trigger too.
Slide 6: No seller has to hand-build outreach per signal.
Slide 7: Trigger plus relevant copy makes personalization work at scale.

lesson.title: Signals Need Messages, Not Just Alerts
takeaways: Intent signals are most useful as triggers for specific plays, not just things to watch.
Customizing the copy to the trigger is as important as detecting the trigger.
Automating both the action and the message removes manual seller work and makes outreach relevant at scale.
lesson.exercise: Pick one intent signal you track today. Write down what action it triggers and what message goes out. If a seller has to write that message manually, draft a copy template that adapts to the signal.
